newsitem.title: RUSSIA: E.Europe economic growth hit by slower exports.
newsitem.headline: E.Europe economic growth hit by slower exports.

text.p: Growth in the emerging economies of central and eastern Europe slowed in 1996, mainly because of a slowdown in exports, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said on Thursday.
But export growth to Western markets seems to have picked up towards the end of this year, the OECD said in its semi-annual economic outlook.
Output growth is seen slowing to three percent from four in Romania next year, to five percent from six in Slovakia but accelerating to three percent from 2.5 in Slovenia.
The decline in Gross Domestic Product in Bulgaria is seen slowing to three percent next year from nine percent in 1996.
The main reason for the slowdown in exports is the sensitivity of the business cycles in the countries' main markets, especially Germany.

The transition to free-market economies has left unused capacity and large stocks of intermediate goods in heavy industries. These, along with low wage and energy costs, allowed exports to boom in 1994 and 1995, the report said.
"But many of these heavy industries remain unrestructured and the sustainability of their export performance is uncertain," the OECD said.
Apart from Bulgaria and Romania, most countries have managed to cut inflation.
"This has been achieved by tight monetary policies and improved credibility of the central banks. Tight control over public spending has also been essential," the survey said.
Inflation is seen falling further in 1997 in all the countries covered except Slovakia, where inflation is seen steady at six percent.
The OECD said banking sectors remain exposed to real systemic risk and highlighted the financial crisis in Bulgaria.
"Depending on the country, either the financial sector has not yet been restructured and remains highly concentrated or many new private banks have been created on an unsound basis."
In the wake of the crisis in Bulgaria, caused by accommodating refinance policies towards distressed banks and an effort to cut interest rates, the government has accelerated structural reforms.
Inflation there of 220-250 percent this year is seen falling to 100 percent in 1997.
GDP growth will slow in Romania, mainly supported by domestic demand, though exports recovered towards the end of 1995.
Rapid recovery continued in Slovakia in 1996 and public spending seems under control. However, the slowdown in export growth could be a risk for a small open economy, the OECD says.

"Unless foreign capital inflows, in particular foreign direct investment, gain more momentum, this could at some point become a constraint on imports of investment goods and, ultimately, on economic growth," the OECD said.
Slowing exports saw output growth fall in Slovenia in 1996.
"Nonethless, economic activity -- including exports -- seems now to be picking up again."
